Predicting whole-framework synthesizability remains notoriously complex because crystallization depends on experimental factors such as solvent selection, temperature, and reagent concentrations. SynthABLE addresses this by decomposing relaxed frameworks into isolated linkers, generating approximately 180,000 unique organic linkers, of which only 73 had been experimentally reported in historical literature.
Structures were prerelaxed using MACE-OMat-D4 and subsequently subjected to two successive density functional theory stages: an initial coarse relaxation using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof generalized gradient approximation with D4 dispersion corrections, followed by rigorous refinement using the meta-GGA r2SCAN-D4 functional.

context.snippet: All electronic structure calculations were performed with plane wave DFT in the Vienna ab initio simulation package78–81. We used two approximations for the exchange-correlation energy: the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation (GGA)38 and r2SCAN meta-GGA39. Although r2SCAN captures some intermediate-range dispersion interactions implicitly, we augmented both PBE and r2SCAN with an explicit D4 dispersion correction82,83. An initial relaxation was performed with PBE-D4; converged wavefunctions were then used to initialize an r2SCAN-D4 relaxation, and these converged wavefunctions were in turn used to compute an r2SCAN-D4 single-point at the optimized geometry to obtain well-converged properties such as the electronic density of states. We generally used the MP24RelaxSet as implemented in the pymatgen Python package84, but made simplifications to accommodate the complexity of these larger MOFs. Total energies were converged within 10−5 eV; forces in the PBE-D4 relaxation within 0.1 eV Å−1, and forces within the r2SCAN-D4 relaxation within 0.05 eV Å−1; we used a plane wave energy cutoff of 680 eV and Gaussian smearing of the Fermi surface with width 0.05 eV. Except in a few cases where a higher k-point density was used to initially test the sensitivity of the calculations to the k-mesh, only the Γ-point was used. The most recent ‘PBE 64’ pseudopotentials (POTCARs) were used. Because the diffusion-generated MOF structures were far from the DFT-optimized structures, we prerelaxed all structures using MACE-OMat-D4 (trained to the OMat24 database of PBE and PBE + U calculations85). Because coordinates produced by diffusion models initially deviate from equilibrium, the generated lattices undergo rapid prescreening and relaxation through a low-level quantum mechanical agent designated as QForge. Implemented in the atomate2 workflow, QForge screens candidates with Zeo++ under specific geometric criteria: frameworks must possess a pore-limiting diameter exceeding 2.5 angstroms, an accessible volume fraction exceeding 30 percent, and an accessible pore volume exceeding nonaccessible space. jina.title: MOFGPT: Generative Design of Metal-Organic Frameworks using Language Models
jina.snippet:
Rishikesh Magar Akshay Antony Radheesh Sharma Meda Amir Barati Farimani

###### Abstract

The discovery of Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs) with application-specific properties remains a central challenge in materials chemistry, owing to the immense size and complexity of their structural design space. Conventional computational screening techniques such as molecular simulations and density functional theory (DFT), while accurate, are computationally prohibitive at scale. Machine learning offers an exciting alternative by leveraging data-driven approaches to accelerate materials discovery. The complexity of MOFs, with their extended periodic structures and diverse topologies, creates both opportunities and challenges for generative modeling approaches. To address these challenges, we present a reinforcement learning-enhanced, transformer-based framework for the de novo design of MOFs. Central to our approach is MOFid, a chemically-informed string representation encoding both connectivity and topology, enabling scalable generative modeling. Our pipeline comprises three components: (1) a generative GPT model trained on MOFid sequences, (2) MOFormer, a transformer-based property predictor, and (3) a reinforcement learning (RL) module that optimizes generated candidates via property-guided reward functions. By integrating property feedback into sequence generation, our method drives the model toward synthesizable, topologically valid MOFs with desired functional attributes. This work demonstrates the potential of large language models, when coupled with reinforcement learning, to accelerate inverse design in reticular chemistry and unlock new frontiers in computational MOF discovery.

###### keywords

Metal-Organic Frameworks, Generative Modeling, Reinforcement Learning, Deep Learning, Material Design

Here we present MOFGen, a system of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) comprising interconnected agents: a large language model that proposes MOF compositions, a diffusion model that generates crystal structures, quantum mechanical agents that optimize and filter candidates, and synthetic-feasibility agents guided by expert rules and machine learning. Trained on a broad set of experimentally reported MOFs and computational databases, MOFGen generated hundreds of thousands of MOF structures and synthesizable organic linkers. The uniqueness of our approach lies in its ability to generate large MOF structures with atomic precision, beyond the scale of conventional generative models limited to tens of atoms. This approach was validated through high-throughput experiments and the successful synthesis of four ‘AI-dreamt’ MOFs.

(4) QForge: a sequence of geometry optimization and Monte Carlo sampling to filter nonporous structures. The structures then undergo a two-stage DFT optimization using the Vienna ab initio simulation package: an initial coarse geometry optimization using the PBE functional with D4 dispersion correction, followed by a tight optimization with r2SCAN-D4.

keenable.title: Agentic AI System Discovers and Synthesizes New Metal-Organic Framework
keenable.snippet:
A modular agentic artificial intelligence system called MOFGen has designed and experimentally realized new porous metal-organic frameworks, uniting generative language models, diffusion networks, quantum mechanical simulations, and high-throughput laboratory robotics. Metal-organic frameworks represent a versatile class of porous crystalline materials composed of inorganic metal nodes linked by organic bridging molecules,

To address these challenges, researchers constructed an interconnected seven-stage agentic workflow capable of proposing full-framework crystal structures with atomic precision, screening structural porosity, evaluating synthetic feasibility, and validating four targeted coordination networks through automated laboratory synthesis.

At the beginning of the pipeline, a coordinating large language model agent named MOFMaster manages system interactions and serves as the user interface, offering three generation pathways: producing structures without chemical constraints, targeting a designated metal secondary building unit, or generating frameworks matching specified compositions. Instructions from MOFMaster pass to LinkerGen, a dedicated language model agent that generates chemical formulae for organic linkers using in-context learning and chain-of-thought prompting informed by reported experimental bridging units.

Electronic formation energies calculated at the r2SCAN-D4 level exhibited negative distributions closely aligning with Materials Project data, affirming physical stability across diverse topological arrangements.

Through a collaboration between Google DeepMind and MOFGen, the largest synthesized set of AI-designed materials to date has been realized. octen.snippet:
To date, tens of thousands of MOFs have been synthesized,, and virtually unlimited more can be proposed based on different combinations of inorganic and organic building blocks.

Given the vast combinatorial space of plausible structures, computational methods have emerged as an efficient means of identifying top-performing MOFs for a given application. − However, there remains a large disconnect between promising MOFs designed on the computer and those that have been successfully realized in the laboratory setting, a challenge that is likely to grow with the advent of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) methods for MOF design. More broadly, despite the enormous interest in MOFs from both computational and experimental scientists, much remains unknown about what factors govern MOF stability and what limits may exist with regards to their synthesizability.

There are numerous factors that collectively influence MOF stability, including but not limited to stability with respect to thermal, chemical, and mechanical stimuli. From a computational standpoint, several machine learning models have been developed to rapidly predict the temperature stability, solvent removal stability, water stability,, and mechanical stability of a given MOF. Another closely connected research direction involves developing heuristics to assess the likelihood of a MOF being synthesizable. With this goal in mind, molecular dynamics simulations have been used to identify bounds of synthesizability based on the free energy required to switch a MOF from an artificial Einstein crystal to a force field representation. , Furthermore, prior work has shown that the degree of linker strain within the MOF unit cell can be used as a metric for its likelihood of synthesizability.

DOI: 10.1021/acsmaterialslett.6c00911
Authors: François‐Xavier Coudert
Published: ACS Materials Letters, 2026-09-18; vol. 8(10)
Type: article
Topics: Metal-Organic Frameworks: Synthesis and Applications; metal-organic frameworks; computational materials design; enthalpy of formation; free energy; phase stability; solvent effects; structural strain; mechanical stability; machine learning; materials screening
Cited by: 0

Abstract

Abstract The growing number of hypothetical metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) has created a need for reliable methods to identify candidates that can be synthesized experimentally. This Viewpoint examines current computational approaches to the evaluation of MOF synthesizability, grouping them into thermodynamic, strain- and mechanics-based, and data-driven methods. Thermodynamic studies evaluate formation enthalpies or free energies, stability relative to competing phases, and can include solvent effects. Structural approaches quantify linker deformation and mechanical stability as a proxy for viability of a hypothetical structure. Data-driven machine learning models use geometric, topological, or chemical relationships to known materials as a way to estimate synthesizability. We review the recent advances of these approaches, their strengths and their limitations, noting that at the present time, there is no silver bullet to solve this open challenge. Future progress will require combining complementary methods and using consistent experimental data to refine computational models and allow the identification of candidates for synthesis in screening studies.

Title:The role of decomposition reactions in assessing first-principles predictions of solid stability
View PDFAbstract:The performance of density functional theory(DFT)approximations for predicting materials thermodynamics is typically assessed by comparing calculated and experimentally determined enthalpies of formation from elemental phases,{\Delta}Hf.However,a compound competes thermodynamically with both other compounds and their constituent elemental forms,and thus,the enthalpies of the decomposition reactions to these competing phases,{\Delta}Hd,determines thermodynamic stability.We evaluated the phase diagrams for 56,791 compounds to classify decomposition reactions into three types:1.those that produce elemental phases,2.those that produce compounds,and 3.those that produce both.This analysis shows that the decomposition into elemental forms is rarely the competing reaction that determines compound stability and that approximately two-thirds of decomposition reactions involve no elemental phases.Using experimentally reported formation enthalpies for 1,012 solid compounds,we assess the accuracy of the generalized gradient approximation(GGA)(PBE)and meta-GGA(SCAN)density functionals for predicting compound stability.For 646 decomposition reactions that are not trivially the formation reaction,PBE(MAD=70 meV/atom)and SCAN(MAD=59 meV/atom)perform similarly,and commonly employed correction schemes using fitted elemental reference energies make only a negligible improvement(~2 meV/atom).Furthermore,for 231 reactions involving only compounds(Type 2),the agreement between SCAN,PBE,and experiment is within~35 meV/atom and is thus comparable to the magnitude of experimental uncertainty.

The synergy between AI and our knowledge of MOFs has the power to revolutionize the way we design and produce materials  [52 ]. One recent example of how to accelerate the discovery of MOFs is the system of an agentic AI called MOFGen, which generated hundreds of thousands of novel MOF structures  [53 ]. Rather than relying on traditional chemical methods, which are often time-consuming and dependent on experimental heuristics and chemical intuition, MOFGen links specialized agents to facilitate the rapid exploration and discovery of synthesizable MOFs. Unlike traditional AI tools, which often rely on structured instructions and close supervision, an agentic AI is known for its ability to make sophisticated decisions in dynamic situations, enabling it to operate effectively in evolving environments with minimal human supervision  [54 ]. MOFGen is a modular system composed of AI and computational agents, each defined as an entity that can act based on its environment to accelerate the discovery of novel MOFs ( Figure 2 ). MOFGen combines large language models that propose novel MOF compositions, diffusion models that generate crystal structures, quantum mechanical agents that optimize and filter candidates, and synthetic-feasibility agents guided by expert rules and machine learning. By employing generative models and AI-driven methodologies, MOFGen accelerates the creation of “AI-dreamt” MOFs ( Figure 2 ). The robustness of MOFGen was experimentally validated by synthesizing five “AI-dreamt” MOFs, whose crystal structures were in agreement with those generated by a diffusion model  [53 ]. 生成模型和机器学习有望加速金属有机框架（metal-organic frameworks，MOFs）在CO
2
捕集和水收集方面的材料发现，但在导航广阔化学空间的同时确保可合成性面临巨大挑战。研究人员在此提出MOFGen，一种智能体人工智能（artificial intelligence，AI）系统，由相互连接的智能体组成：一个提出MOF组成的大型语言模型，一个生成晶体结构的扩散模型，优化和过滤候选材料的量子力学智能体，以及由专家规则和机器学习引导的合成可行性智能体。
研究人员在广泛实验报道的MOF和计算数据库上训练，MOFGen生成了数十万个MOF结构和可合成的有机连接子。研究人员方法的独特之处在于能够以原子精度生成大型MOF结构，超越了仅限于数十个原子的传统生成模型的规模。通过高通量实验和四个'AI梦'MOF的成功合成验证了该方法。
金属有机框架（metal-organic frameworks，MOFs）是由金属节点与有机配体通过强键连接形成的纳米多孔晶体材料，在二氧化碳（CO
2
）捕集和水收集等全球性挑战中具有重要应用前景。然而，传统MOF发现依赖试错法、经验启发和化学直觉，其合成通常需要筛选大量实验条件，且多步有机配体合成过程劳动密集，严重限制了化学空间的探索。
尽管生成模型和机器学习已在无机材料生成中取得突破，但MOF结构大、组成复杂、拓扑多样，现有生成模型仅能处理数十个原子的体系，且缺乏对可合成性的系统考虑。为此，研究人员开发了MOFGen——一种由多个智能体组成的智能体人工智能（artificial intelligence，AI）系统，旨在加速可合成MOF的发现，并验证了其在实验室中的可行性。
研究人员利用实验数据库CoRE MOF 2019、剑桥结构数据库（CSD）以及计算数据库ultra MOF、BW-DB、QMOF和ToBaCCo共约500,000个MOF训练系统。
关键技术包括：LLM智能体LinkerGen通过上下文学习和链式思考生成配体化学式；全原子去噪扩散模型CrystalGen以化学式为条件生成晶体结构；低层级量子力学智能体QForge使用MACE-
MP-0和GFN1-xTB进行预优化和筛选；SynthABLE分解MOF并利用Allchemy和多种合成评分评估可合成性；高层级量子力学智能体QHarden依次执行PBE-D4和r2SCAN-D4的DFT优化；SynthGen平台进行高通量合成，并采用PXRD或SCXRD表征。通过上述方法，研究人员生成了259,559个预测MOF结构，并成功验证了四个'AI梦'MOF。
MOFGen概述：MOFGen由多个相互连接的智能体组成。主智能体MOFMaster提供三种生成选项：无化学信息生成、含特定金属次级构筑单元（secondary building unit，SBU）生成、给定组成生成。指令传递给LinkerGen产生化学式，再由CrystalGen生成结构，依次经QForge、SynthABLE、QHarden筛选，最终由SynthGen进行合成验证。该系统实现了从计算预测到实验室实现的快速路径。
LinkerGen化学式生成：LinkerGen采用SMILES到SMILES策略，结合链式思考提示，确保化学计量比正确。与零样本生成相比，上下文学习生成的配体SCScore分布（平均2.47）与实验数据一致，而零样本生成偏向常见配体（峰值为1.84）。生成的配体化学式与金属SBU组合，并扩展出最多256原子的超胞公式。
CrystalGen晶体结构生成：MOF结构表示为点云，每个原子以分数坐标和原子序数编码。CrystalGen初始化256个随机原子，在去噪过程中删除无关原子并移动相关原子，在无分类器引导下按化学式生成结构。针对锌基MOF（Zn
4
O SBU），每个化学式生成10个候选，共生成259,559个预测MOF结构，表明点云方法能有效捕捉MOF的几何与化学多样性。

PRO-MOF decomposes the inverse design of Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs) into a two-layer strategy: "selecting chemical building blocks first, then assembling 3D structures." Generative models and machine learning promise accelerated material discovery in metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) for CO2 capture and water harvesting, but face substantial challenges in navigating vast chemical spaces while ensuring synthesizability. Here we present MOFGen, a system of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) comprising interconnected agents: a large language model that proposes MOF compositions, a diffusion model that generates crystal structures, quantum mechanical agents that optimize and filter candidates, and synthetic-feasibility agents guided by expert rules and machine learning. ## What a generative nanomaterial design workflow actually is in 2026

A generative nanomaterial design workflow is a connected sequence of computational steps that proposes candidate nanostructures, predicts their properties, filters for synthesizability, and hands the survivors to a wet-lab or fabrication team. As of mid-2026 the most productive setups are not single models but pipelines that combine an inverse-design generator (often a diffusion model, variational autoencoder, or graph neural network), a property-prediction surrogate, a synthesizability or thermodynamic filter, and an automated synthesis-and-characterization loop. Surveys of AI for science and engineering discovery published in 2024 and 2025 consistently place these pipelines among the fastest-moving subfields, alongside AI-driven protein design and catalyst discovery. The reason is straightforward: nanoparticle, 2D-material, and metal-organic-framework design spaces are too large for human intuition or brute-force screening, and property predictors now reach accuracy levels where they can replace a meaningful fraction of early-stage DFT or experimental screening.

The integration of uncertainty quantification (UQ), crystal graph representations, and active learning (AL) strategies has become the backbone of modern AI-driven materials discovery platforms. ### **1. Design as building-block assembling**

In the 21st century, society is facing several fundamental challenges, including global climate change, the energy crisis, and public health crises such as cancers and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Their solutions share a certain commonality: They all involve the discovery of novel atomic structures such as materials, molecules, proteins, and drugs. Designing such functional atomic structures is challenging due to the astonishing complexity of their inter-atomic interactions, sophisticated physical/chemical/geometric constraints and patterns in the formation of stable structures, and the relation between structures and their functions.

Like most engineering design activities, the mainstream paradigm of materials design is currently the rational design approach, which emphasizes a causal understanding of the structure-function relationship and depends on heuristic expert knowledge and explicit design rules. The typical "tinkering" design process starts with topology design with a limited number of prototypes and ends with parametric design. ultimate.snippet:
Here we present MOFGen, a system of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) comprising interconnected agents: a large language model that proposes MOF compositions, a diffusion model that generates crystal structures, quantum mechanical agents that optimize and filter candidates, and synthetic-feasibility agents guided by expert rules and machine learning. Trained on a broad set of experimentally reported MOFs and computational databases, MOFGen generated hundreds of thousands of MOF structures and synthesizable organic linkers. The uniqueness of our approach lies in its ability to generate large MOF structures with atomic precision, beyond the scale of conventional generative models limited to tens of atoms. This approach was validated through high-throughput experiments and the successful synthesis of four ‘AI-dreamt’ MOFs.

ultimate.title: Agentic AI System Discovers and Synthesizes New Metal-Organic Framework
ultimate.snippet:
A modular agentic artificial intelligence system called MOFGen has designed and experimentally realized new porous metal-organic frameworks, uniting generative language models, diffusion networks, quantum mechanical simulations, and high-throughput laboratory robotics. Metal-organic frameworks represent a versatile class of porous crystalline materials composed of inorganic metal nodes linked by organic bridging molecules,

To address these challenges, researchers constructed an interconnected seven-stage agentic workflow capable of proposing full-framework crystal structures with atomic precision, screening structural porosity, evaluating synthetic feasibility, and validating four targeted coordination networks through automated laboratory synthesis.

At the beginning of the pipeline, a coordinating large language model agent named MOFMaster manages system interactions and serves as the user interface, offering three generation pathways: producing structures without chemical constraints, targeting a designated metal secondary building unit, or generating frameworks matching specified compositions. Instructions from MOFMaster pass to LinkerGen, a dedicated language model agent that generates chemical formulae for organic linkers using in-context learning and chain-of-thought prompting informed by reported experimental bridging units.

Electronic formation energies calculated at the r2SCAN-D4 level exhibited negative distributions closely aligning with Materials Project data, affirming physical stability across diverse topological arrangements.
